loText: Estimate contingent liquidity via the liquid asset buffer.
question: The chief risk officer of a mid-sized commercial bank is presenting to newly hired risk analysts on how the bank’s liquidity stress test is built. She wants one slide that defines contingent liquidity precisely and states what the stress test is principally trying to measure. Which of the following statements best describes contingent liquidity and its role in the liquidity stress test?

options.A: Contingent liquidity is the cash needed to fund the business daily and ensure orderly clearing of payments; it is held in the liquid asset buffer, and the stress test’s principal objective is to measure how much of it is required to cover stressed cash outflows.
options.B: Contingent liquidity is the liquidity available to meet general financial obligations under a stress scenario; it is held in the liquid asset buffer, and the stress test’s principal objective is to project the bank’s capital ratios under a recessionary scenario.
options.C: Contingent liquidity is the liquidity available to meet general financial obligations under a stress scenario; it is held in the liquid asset buffer, and the stress test’s principal objective is to measure how much of it is required to cover stressed cash outflows.
options.D: Contingent liquidity is the liquidity available to meet general financial obligations under a stress scenario; it is held in a buffer that may include any security the bank owns, because the stress scenario already captures how quickly each security can be sold.

solution:
CRO slide for new analysts: define contingent liquidity and the stress test’s principal objective.

GARP frames the liquidity stress test around funding liquidity risk: the risk that the institution will not have adequate capacity to fund its obligations without incurring unacceptable economic losses. Within funding liquidity, institutions use liquidity for four purposes, and only one of them is meant to absorb a crisis:

| Type | What it is for | Available for general obligations under stress? |
|---|---|---|
| Operational | Daily business needs, orderly clearing of payments | No: needed to keep operating |
| Restricted | Specifically defined purposes, e.g. collateralization | No (applied only to the outflows it supports) |
| Contingent | General financial obligati […]

question:
A senior risk analyst at a U.S. bank holding company is validating the criteria that securities must meet to be included in the liquid asset buffer used in the liquidity stress test. The draft policy lists the following criteria:

I. The securities should have low credit and market risk and offer ease and certainty of valuation.

II. The securities should trade in an active and sizable market with a high concentration of buyers and sellers, so that a few dominant dealers can absorb large sales.

III. The requirements should ensure that the liquidity-generating capacity of the securities remains intact even in periods of severe idiosyncratic and market stress.

IV. The securities may be held and controlled by any business line, provided the business line reports the holdings to treasury each month.

Which of the criteria are consistent with the reading?

options.A: I only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: I, III and IV only
options.D: I and III only

solution:
U.S. BHC validation: which liquid asset buffer eligibility criteria are consistent with GARP.

**Concept and theory**

Because the buffer is the bank’s contingent liquidity, the quality of the estimate depends on what is allowed into it. GARP (Section 9.2) requires the framework to clearly define the market and operational characteristics that securities must meet to qualify. The governing principle is that the liquidity-generating capacity of buffer securities must remain intact even in periods of severe idiosyncratic and market stress, because the buffer is precisely what is drawn on in those periods.

A prudential regulator in Australia is reviewing a bank’s AUD liquidity stress test submission. The bank’s scenario assumes that market conditions limit realized inflows to a fixed proportion of contractual inflows, and the regulator applies an LCR-style cap under which recognized inflows may not exceed 75% of stressed outflows.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Normal liquid asset buffer (AUD million) | 2,150 |
| Stressed outflows, all categories (AUD million) | 1,800 |

I. The report is tracked weekly and monthly because it gives an idea of the LTD ratio in the immediate short term.

| Quarter-end | Q1 | Q2 | Q3 | Q4 |

| Head office undrawn commitments | 2,140 | 2,310 | 2,585 | 2,790 |

| Total undrawn commitments | 2,750 | 2,950 | 3,290 | 3,550 |
| Aggregate limit | 3,800 | 3,800 | 3,800 | 3,800 |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bank K | 18 | 27 | 46 | 78 | 115 |

loText: Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).
question: A credit analyst is evaluating the liquidity of a small regional bank while preparing a report for a credit committee meeting. With quarterly financial statements, the analyst calculates some relevant liquidity indicators over the past three years. Which of the following trends over this period should the analyst be most concerned about in the credit risk report?

options.A: The bank’s average net federal funds and repurchase agreements position has been increasing.
options.B: The bank’s capacity ratio has been increasing.
options.C: The bank’s pledged securities ratio has been decreasing.
options.D: The bank’s loan commitments ratio has been decreasing.

solution:
**Concept**

Liquidity indicators. Capacity ratio = net loans and leases / total assets: a higher ratio means less liquidity, because loans are illiquid. Other indicators: cash position, liquid securities, net federal funds and repo position, pledged securities ratio, loan commitments ratio.

**Exam trap.** Polarity varies by indicator. For the capacity, pledged securities and loan commitments ratios, an increase is bad for liquidity. For the net federal funds position, an increase is good.

loText: Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity.
question: A bank plans to purchase a newly issued 1-year bond with a face value of GBP 20 million. The bond has an annualized coupon rate of 8%, paid semi-annually, and is priced at 102% of par. A treasury analyst is asked to describe the impact of this purchase on the term structure of expected cash flows (TSECF) and the term structure of available assets (TSAA). Which of the following correctly describes the change in both the TSECF and the TSAA with a 7-month time horizon at the time the purchase is made?

options.A: The TSECF will decrease by GBP 20 million and the TSAA will increase by GBP 20.4 million.
options.B: The TSECF will decrease by GBP 19.6 million and the TSAA will increase by GBP 20 million.
options.C: The TSECF will increase by GBP 19.6 million and the TSAA will decrease by GBP 20 million.
options.D: The TSECF will increase by GBP 20 million and the TSAA will decrease by GBP 20.4 million.

solution:
**Concept**

The term structure of expected cash flows (TSECF) records the cash a transaction pays and receives within the horizon. The term structure of available assets (TSAA) records the securities available to generate liquidity. Buying a bond lowers cash and raises available assets.

**Exam trap.** Direction and amount. The TSAA rises by the face amount of the bond; the TSECF falls by the price paid less any coupon received inside the horizon.

loText: Differentiate between various types of liquidity, including funding, operational, strategic, contingent, and restricted liquidity.
question: A junior treasury analyst at a bank is asked to classify assets held by the bank into different types of liquidity to assess potential funding sources for a liquidity stress test. The analyst evaluates both on-balance sheet assets and off-balance sheet assets to determine the proper classification of liquidity. Which of the following correctly describes an example of restricted liquidity?

options.A: High-quality liquid assets required to fund the bank’s day-to-day operations
options.B: Cash and money-market instruments allocated to finance the bank’s expansion into new geographic regions
options.C: A position in mortgage-backed securities held within a special purpose vehicle established by the bank
options.D: US Treasury notes pledged as collateral against a large wholesale loan taken by the bank

solution:
**Concept**

Types of liquidity. Funding: to meet obligations as they fall due. Operational: for day-to-day business. Strategic: to pursue strategic objectives. Contingent: available to survive a stress. Restricted: tied to a specific purpose, such as collateral pledged against a loan, and so not available for general use.

**Exam trap.** Pledged assets are liquid instruments that the bank cannot use. The label depends on availability, not on asset quality.

loText: Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.
question: A liquidity risk manager at a bank is holding a seminar for a group of newly hired risk analysts. The manager makes a presentation on liquidity risk reporting and stress testing and also compares the different types of liquidity risk reports. Which of the following statements about liquidity risk reports is correct for the manager to make?

options.A: The funding gap report identifies the concentration of funding providers for the bank.
options.B: The undrawn commitments report identifies the off-balance sheet products that the bank may be required to fund.
options.C: The wholesale pricing and volume report identifies the maturity gaps between all the assets and liabilities of the bank.
options.D: The liability profile report identifies the time horizon when the bank’s cumulative cash flow becomes negative.

solution:
**Concept**

Liquidity reports and what each shows. Funding concentration: reliance on particular providers. Funding maturity gap: mismatches between asset and liability maturities. Undrawn commitments: off-balance-sheet items the bank may have to fund. Cash flow survival horizon: when cumulative cash flow turns negative.

**Exam trap.** Each wrong option attaches one report’s purpose to another report’s name. Learn them as name and purpose pairs.
